title: Install Laminate Flooring
summary: Install a floating click-lock laminate floor over wood or concrete, with the right underlayment, even expansion gaps and clean transitions.
safety: Saw laminate outside or in a ventilated area with safety glasses, an N95 mask and hearing protection: its dust is fine and hard. Keep hands clear of blades and unplug saws to change blades. Wear knee pads. Don't sand or scrape old vinyl or its glue: it may contain asbestos.
pro: the subfloor is rotten or very uneven, the slab shows moisture, the old flooring may contain asbestos, or you're doing stairs. Floating floors generally don't need a permit.

questions.label: Sq ft per box (on the label)
Plank face width
questions.hint: Measure the visible face, not the tongue.

calcNote: Row widths assume a square room with planks running along the length. Check with a tape at both ends before cutting. Poly allows 8" seam overlaps and 2" up each wall.

tools.w: Buy all boxes at once from the same lot so colors match. Check the AC rating (AC3+ for most homes).

tools.n: Laminate underlayment (foam or 2-in-1 with vapor barrier)
tools.w: Required unless the planks have a pad attached. Cushions, quiets and evens out tiny bumps.
tools.q: {{a.sub==='concrete'?'laminate underlayment vapor barrier':'laminate underlayment foam'}} 100 sq ft

tools.w: Vapor barrier over concrete, unless your underlayment already has one built in.
Fills dips and seams so the floor is flat enough.
Fixes squeaks and loose panels before you cover them.
Covers edges at doorways and other floors. Buy the ones made to match your laminate.
Only if the old baseboard can't go back low enough to hide the gap.
Reattach baseboard to the wall.
Seals the gap at tubs, door frames and pipes in damp areas.

tools.n: Tape measure, pencil, chalk line, string
tools.w: Measuring, marking and keeping the first row straight.
Marks square cuts.
Finds high and low spots in the subfloor.

tools.n: {{a.saw==='miter'?'Miter saw':'Circular saw'}} with a fine-tooth or laminate blade
tools.w: Laminate is too hard to score and snap. Cuts plank ends and long rips.
Notches, curves and cut-outs.
Holes for pipes; driving subfloor screws.
Undercuts door casing so planks slide under.

tools.n: Flooring kit: tapping block, pull bar, spacers
tools.w: Closes joints without damaging edges; keeps the expansion gap.
tools.q: flooring installation kit tapping block pull bar

tools.w: Taps the block and bar.

tools.n: Flat pry bar + wide putty knife
tools.w: Removes baseboard without denting the wall.
Cutting dust and grit must be cleaned up before planks go down.
Takes down high seams on wood subfloors.

tools.n: Wide flat trowel or 10" taping knife
tools.w: Spreads floor patch.

tools.n: Brad nailer or hammer + nail set
tools.w: Reinstalls baseboard.

tools.n: Safety glasses, hearing protection, N95 dust mask, knee pads
tools.w: Sawing laminate throws fine, hard dust and is loud.

steps.t: Measure the room and buy the flooring
steps.idea: Buy enough laminate from one lot, plus the underlayment it needs.
steps.b:
1. Measure the length and width of the room wall to wall at the widest points. Enter them on the Start tab.
  2. Add closets and alcoves into the size (or work them out separately and add the boxes).
  3. Enter the "sq ft per box" from the box label.
  4. Pick waste: 10% for a simple room, 15% for lots of corners or angles.
  5. Buy {{c.boxes}} boxes{{a.pad==='separate'?', '+c.rolls+' rolls of underlayment':''}}{{a.sub==='concrete'?' and 6-mil poly (or an underlayment with a built-in vapor barrier)':''}}.
  6. Check every box shows the same lot number. Keep one spare box after the job.
faq: Abrasion class: how tough the wear layer is. AC3 suits most rooms in a home, AC4 is better for busy areas and entries.
Thicker (10–12 mm) feels and sounds more solid and hides small bumps better, but it raises the floor more at doorways.

steps.t: Read the install instructions and check the room
steps.idea: Laminate brands set the gap, the underlayment, the largest room size and where it's allowed. Breaking those rules voids the warranty.
steps.b:
1. Find the instruction sheet in a box or on the maker's site.
  2. Write down: the expansion gap (enter it on the Start tab), the flatness limit, the underlayment rule, and the maximum run length before a T-molding break.
  3. Check if the maker requires a T-molding at every doorway. Many do.
  4. Check the rooms it's rated for. Standard laminate is not for bathrooms, laundry rooms or anywhere water can stand.
  5. Check the subfloor rules for your floor type (concrete, plywood, radiant heat).
steps.stop: {{a.room==='wet'?'Standard laminate swells permanently when water gets into the joints. In a bathroom or laundry room use only laminate rated waterproof by its maker, and follow its extra steps (often silicone at the perimeter). Otherwise choose LVP or tile.':'Wet areas (bathrooms, laundry) need laminate rated waterproof by the maker. In a kitchen or entry, wipe spills right away and use mats at the sink and door.'}}

steps.t: Bring the boxes in to acclimate
steps.idea: Laminate is wood fiber. It needs to settle to the room's humidity and temperature before it's installed.
steps.wait: Acclimate as long as the box says (often 48 hours)
steps.b:
1. Run the heat or AC at normal living settings. Keep it there during and after the install.
  2. Stack the closed boxes flat in the room (not the garage or basement), a few inches apart, away from vents and sunny windows.
  3. Leave them unopened for the time on the box, usually 48 hours.
  4. Don't install in a freshly painted, drywalled or very humid room. Let it dry first.

steps.t: Empty the room and remove baseboard
steps.idea: Baseboard comes off so the floor runs under it and hides the gap.
steps.b:
1. Move the furniture out. Take off doors that swing over the floor (tap the hinge pins up and out).
  2. Remove floor vent covers.
  3. Cut the paint line along the top of the baseboard with a utility knife.
  4. Slide a wide putty knife against the wall, then the pry bar in front of it. Pry a little at each nail, moving along the board.
  5. Number each piece on the back and on the wall above it.
  6. Pull nails out through the back with pliers.
faq: Can I leave the baseboard on?
Yes, then cover the gap with shoe molding or quarter-round nailed to the baseboard. Make sure it's wide enough to cover a {{frac(a.gap)}} gap plus a little.

steps.t: Pull up the carpet and pad
steps.idea: Laminate needs a hard, flat base: carpet, pad, tack strip and staples all come out.
steps.b:
1. Pull up a corner of carpet with pliers and peel it off the tack strip.
  2. Cut it into 3 ft strips with a utility knife, roll and tape them.
  3. Pull up the pad and remove every staple.
  4. Pry up the tack strip. Gloves on: the tacks are sharp.
  5. Sweep and vacuum.

steps.idea: Laminate can float over some flat, solid floors, but not over anything soft.
steps.b:
1. Old vinyl or tile must be one layer, firmly stuck and flat. Cushioned vinyl, carpet and other floating floors come out.
  2. Fill deep grout lines on old tile with floor patch.
  3. Check doors and appliances still clear the higher floor.
steps.stop: Vinyl flooring and black adhesive from before about 1980 may contain asbestos. Don't sand, scrape or tear it out. Float over it, or have it tested first.

steps.idea: Trim the bottom of the casing so planks slide under it, instead of notching around it.
steps.b:
1. Lay a scrap of underlayment, then a scrap plank face down on it, against the casing.
  2. Rest the jamb saw flat on the scrap, blade against the casing.
  3. Saw straight in with long steady strokes.
  4. Cut both sides of every opening and any door stop that reaches the floor.
  5. Knock out the cut piece and vacuum.
  6. Test: a plank slides under with room for the expansion gap.

steps.idea: Squeaks under laminate stay forever. Fix them now.
steps.b:
1. Walk the floor slowly and mark squeaks and soft spots with tape.
  2. Find the joists (rows of nails, usually 16" apart).
  3. Drive a 1-5/8" screw into the joist beside each squeak, head just below the surface.
  4. Set any nail heads that stick up.
steps.stop: Soft, stained or spongy subfloor is rotten. Cut it out and replace it before you continue.

steps.idea: Laminate bridges small bumps but flexes over dips, and flexing breaks the joints.
steps.b:
1. Sweep the floor.
  2. Slide the straightedge across the floor in rows, then at 90°.
  3. Circle spots where it rocks (high) and outline spots with light under it (low).
  4. Compare with your sheet's limit, often about 3/16" in 10 ft.

steps.t: Sand high spots, patch low spots
steps.idea: Bring the bumps down and fill the dips so the floor lies flat.
steps.b:
1. Sand high seams on wood with 40-grit until the straightedge sits flat.
  2. On concrete, grind high spots with a rented grinder or rub brick. Wear a silica-rated mask.
  3. Mix floor patch to peanut-butter thickness and trowel it into the lows, feathering the edges.
  4. Let it harden (check the bag), check again, add a thin second coat if needed.
  5. Sand ridges smooth and vacuum.

steps.idea: A damp slab will swell laminate from below.
steps.b:
1. Tape an 18" x 18" piece of clear plastic tight to the slab on all four edges. Do 2–3 spots.
  2. Wait at least 16 hours.
  3. Water drops or a darker spot under it means too wet: fix the moisture first.
  4. Do any measured test your maker requires (calcium chloride or RH) and compare to its limit.
steps.stop: A basement slab that's ever had water on it is risky for laminate. Consider LVP rated for below grade instead.

steps.idea: Grit under the underlayment becomes a bump or a squeak.
steps.b:
1. Scrape off paint drips, drywall mud and glue lumps.
  2. Vacuum everything, including corners and under the door casings.
  3. Run your hand over the floor: it should feel smooth.

steps.idea: On concrete, a plastic sheet stops ground moisture from reaching the laminate.
steps.b:
1. Skip this if your underlayment has a vapor barrier built in ("2-in-1" or "3-in-1"), but still tape its seams.
  2. Roll out 6-mil poly across the floor.
  3. Overlap every seam by 8" and tape it with packing or seam tape.
  4. Run the edges about 2" up the walls. You'll trim the excess after the baseboard goes back.
  5. Don't puncture it. Walk carefully, and patch holes with tape.
faq: Do I need poly over plywood?
Usually not. Over wood subfloors, poly can trap moisture. Some makers want it over a damp crawlspace; follow your sheet.

steps.idea: Underlayment cushions the laminate, quiets footsteps and smooths out tiny bumps.
steps.b:
1. Roll one strip along the starting wall, running the same way as the planks.
  2. Butt the next strip edge to edge. Don't overlap it unless the underlayment has a built-in overlap flap.
  3. Tape every seam.
  4. Only roll out a few strips ahead of the planks so you don't tear them.
steps.stop: If the planks already have a pad attached, don't add another layer (except poly on concrete). Two pads make the floor too soft and the joints break.

steps.t: Pick a direction and the starting wall
steps.idea: Run planks the long way of the room and start along a straight wall.
steps.b:
1. Run planks parallel to the longest wall or toward the main window light.
  2. Pick the longest, straightest wall to start from.
  3. Measure the room width at both ends. A difference over 1/2" means the room is out of square: split it between the first and last rows.
  4. Snap a chalk line or stretch a string one plank-width plus the gap off the wall. If the wall bows more than about 1/4", trace it onto the first-row planks and cut them to match.

steps.t: Plan the first and last rows
steps.idea: Avoid a sliver row along a wall. Thin rows look bad and don't lock well.
steps.b:
1. Measure the visible face width of a plank (Start tab: {{a.pw}}").
  2. About {{c.rows}} rows fit across the room.
  3. First row: {{frac(c.firstRow)}}. Last row: {{frac(c.lastRow)}}.
  4. {{c.rip?'The last row would have been too thin, so rip the first row to that width too (cut off the tongue side).':'No rip on the first row: just cut off the tongue that faces the wall.'}}
  5. Check with a tape at both ends before cutting.

steps.idea: Laminate moves more than vinyl. It needs a gap at every wall and, in big areas, a break.
steps.b:
1. Your gap is {{frac(a.gap)}} at every wall, door frame, pipe, cabinet and hearth.
  2. Measure the longest run in each direction. If it's longer than the maker's maximum, plan a T-molding break there.
  3. If your maker requires it, plan a T-molding in each doorway between rooms ({{a.doors}} on your list).
  4. Keep cabinets, islands and anything screwed down off the laminate: install them first and float the floor up to them.
faq: Can I run one floor through the whole house?
Only if the maker allows that run length and doesn't require doorway breaks. Otherwise the floor can buckle or open gaps in summer or winter.

steps.t: Set up a safe cutting station
steps.idea: Laminate is cut with a saw, which makes fine, hard dust. Cut outside or in the garage.
steps.b:
1. Set the {{a.saw==='miter'?'miter saw':'circular saw'}} up outside, in a garage or a ventilated spot, on a stable bench.
  2. Fit a fine-tooth (60+ teeth) or laminate blade. A dull or coarse blade chips the face.
  3. {{a.saw==='miter'?'A miter or table saw cuts downward into the top: cut planks face up.':'A circular saw and jigsaw cut upward: cut planks face down.'}}
  4. Wear safety glasses, an N95 mask and hearing protection.
  5. Practice on a scrap: the face edge should be clean, not chipped.
faq: Can I score and snap laminate like vinyl?
No. The core is too hard. A rented laminate cutter (guillotine) works for crosscuts with no dust, but not for long rips.

steps.idea: The first row sets everything. Make it straight and tight.
steps.b:
1. Open 3 or 4 boxes and mix planks from them as you go.
  2. Cut the tongue off the long side facing the wall{{c.rip?' (rip to '+frac(c.firstRow)+')':''}}.
  3. Start in the left corner, groove facing you, cut edge against {{frac(a.gap)}} spacers.
  4. Lock each end joint the way your sheet shows (angle in, or drop and tap).
  5. Measure the last plank in the row (minus the gap) and cut it.
  6. Sight down the row: straight along your string, gap even.
faq: Follow the string, not the wall. Add or remove spacers to keep the row straight.

steps.idea: Offset end joints so the floor locks together strongly and looks natural.
steps.b:
1. Start row 2 with the cut-off from row 1 if it's at least as long as your sheet's minimum (often 8–12").
  2. Keep end joints in neighboring rows at least that far apart.
  3. Angle the long side into the row before at about 20–30° and press it down.
  4. Close end joints with a tapping block, using light taps.
  5. Step back every few rows: no H-joints or stair-steps.

steps.idea: Repeat row by row, keeping joints tight and the gap even.
steps.b:
1. Every few rows, check the first row is still straight and the spacers are in place.
  2. Close gaps only with the tapping block or pull bar. Never hit a plank edge with the mallet.
  3. Look at each plank before you lay it. Put chipped ones aside for closet cuts.
  4. Run your fingers over each joint: flush, no lip, no gap.
  5. Wipe off sawdust as you go so it doesn't get into the joints.
faq: A joint has a peaked ridge.
Something is under it or the lock didn't fully seat. Unclick, clean the groove and relay it. Don't hammer it down.

steps.idea: Undercut casings let the floor run in without visible notches.
steps.b:
1. Measure and mark the notch around the door jamb on the plank.
  2. Cut it with the jigsaw (face down) and test-fit.
  3. Slide it under the casing flat if you can't angle it in, and close the long joint with the pull bar.
  4. Keep the gap under the casing too.
faq: Where I can't angle it, can I glue it?
Yes. Trim the lower lip of the groove off and glue that one joint with the wood glue the maker recommends.

steps.idea: Drill the hole bigger than the pipe so the floor can still move.
steps.b:
1. Mark the pipe center: distance from the wall and from the last row.
  2. Drill a hole 1/2" bigger than the pipe (or the gap size on each side).
  3. Cut from the hole to the plank edge, fit the plank and glue the strip back in behind the pipe.
  4. Cut vent openings to match the duct; the cover sits on top.
  5. Cover the pipe gap with a pipe collar ring.

steps.t: Cut and fit the last row
steps.idea: Mark each last-row plank to match the wall, so the gap stays even.
steps.b:
1. Lay a loose plank (A) exactly on top of the last full row.
  2. Lay another plank (B) over it, pushed against the spacer at the wall.
  3. Draw along B's edge onto A.
  4. Rip A on the line. The strip B didn't cover is the piece that fits.
  5. Click it in and close it with the pull bar.
  6. Remove all spacers.

steps.idea: Moldings cover the edges and let each floor move on its own.
steps.b:
1. T-molding between two floors of the same height and at required doorway or long-run breaks; reducer to a lower floor; end cap against a taller floor or a slider door.
  2. Cut to length with the fine-tooth saw.
  3. Fasten the track to the subfloor in the gap between floors, never through the laminate.
  4. Snap or press the molding in.
  5. Check the floor still slides underneath.

steps.idea: Baseboard hides the gap and is nailed to the wall so the floor can still move.
steps.b:
1. {{a.sub==='concrete'?'Trim the poly sheet just below the top of the floor with a utility knife. ':''}}Match each numbered piece to its spot.
  2. Rest it lightly on the floor, then lift it a paper's thickness.
  3. Nail into the wall studs and bottom plate, not down into the floor.
  4. Shoe molding gets nailed to the baseboard, not the floor.
  5. Fill nail holes and touch up paint.
  6. At tubs and door frames, seal the gap with flexible silicone.

steps.idea: Laminate lasts if you keep water and grit off it.
steps.b:
1. Check every wall, pipe and jamb: no plank is touching.
  2. Rehang doors (trim the bottom if they drag) and vent covers.
  3. Put felt pads under furniture and a mat under rolling chairs.
  4. Put mats at outside doors and at the kitchen sink.
  5. Clean with a dry mop or a barely damp one. Never wet-mop or steam-mop laminate.
  6. Wipe spills right away.
steps.stop: Don't nail, screw or glue the floor down or set fixed cabinets on it. A pinned floating floor buckles.

days.wait: Boxes acclimate in the room (often 48 hours)
Patch dries; concrete moisture test sits overnight
Natural break at the end of the day

sawHelp.b:
1. Use a fine-tooth (60T+) or laminate blade.
  2. Miter or table saw: face up. Circular saw or jigsaw: face down.
  3. Mark on the side facing up, with a square.
  4. Let the blade reach full speed before it touches the plank; feed slowly.
  5. Support both ends so the cut-off doesn't snap and chip.

tapHelp.t: Use a tapping block and pull bar
tapHelp.b:
1. Tapping block: lip against the plank's edge, tap the block with the mallet. Several light taps beat one hard hit.
  2. Pull bar: hook it over the end of a plank next to a wall and tap its raised end toward the joint.
  3. Never hit a laminate edge directly. A crushed lock never closes again.

jambHelp.b:
1. Set underlayment and a plank scrap (face down) against the casing.
  2. Lay the saw flat on top.
  3. Saw with long, light strokes.
  4. Pop out the cut piece.

pryHelp.b:
1. Cut the paint line with a utility knife.
  2. Put a wide putty knife against the wall as a shield.
  3. Pry a little at each nail along the length.
  4. Pull nails through the back with pliers.

patchHelp.b:
1. Mix small batches: patch often hardens in 15–20 minutes.
  2. Press it into the low spot with the trowel held almost flat.
  3. Pull outward past the edges so it thins to nothing.
  4. Sand ridges once hard.

jamb.title: Cut the casing with a jamb saw
jamb.cap: Lay a scrap plank upside down on a piece of underlayment against the casing, rest the saw flat on it and cut. Pull out the cut-off piece.

Lows: fill up.</text><path d="M10 110 L50 110 Q80 92 110 110 L150 110 L150 140 L10 140Z" class="w"/><path d="M50 110 Q80 102 110 110" class="a d" fill="none"/><text x="80" y="84" class="k" text-anchor="middle">high: sand</text><text x="80" y="158" text-anchor="middle">wood seam</text><text x="80" y="170" text-anchor="middle">or ridge</text><path d="M170 100 L210 100 Q240 122 270 100 L310 100 L310 140 L170 140Z" class="b"/><path d="M200 100 L210 100 Q240 122 270 100 L280 100 Z" class="th"/><text x="240" y="84" class="k" text-anchor="middle">low: patch</text><text x="240" y="158" text-anchor="middle">trowel it level,</text><text x="240" y="170" text-anchor="middle">feather the edges</text>
fixes.cap: Feather patch out wide, past the edges of the dip, and sand any ridges once it hardens.

moisture.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Concrete: quick moisture check</text><rect x="10" y="110" width="300" height="50" class="th"/><text x="160" y="140" text-anchor="middle">concrete slab</text><rect x="90" y="100" width="140" height="8" class="mos"/><rect x="84" y="98" width="10" height="12" class="y"/><rect x="226" y="98" width="10" height="12" class="y"/><text x="160" y="90" text-anchor="middle">18" x 18" plastic, edges taped</text><text x="10" y="40" class="k">Leave it 16+ hours. Then look under it:</text><text x="10" y="54">drops or a dark damp spot = too wet.</text><text x="10" y="180">Real numbers need a test kit (see your box).</text>
moisture.cap: The plastic test only catches obvious problems. Many makers ask for a calcium chloride or RH test with a limit printed in the instructions.

gap.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Leave a gap at every wall</text><rect x="246" y="20" width="40" height="140" class="b"/><text x="266" y="36" text-anchor="middle">wall</text><rect x="10" y="140" width="300" height="20" class="w"/><text x="40" y="174">subfloor</text><rect x="10" y="128" width="224" height="12" class="tl"/><text x="30" y="122" class="k">floating plank</text><rect x="234" y="128" width="12" height="12" class="y"/><rect x="228" y="92" width="18" height="48" class="w" fill-opacity="0.85"/><text x="160" y="72" class="ac" text-anchor="middle">baseboard hides the gap</text><line x1="212" y1="76" x2="232" y2="92" class="a"/><text x="240" y="186" class="ac" text-anchor="middle">{{frac(a.gap)}} gap (spacer)</text><line x1="240" y1="176" x2="240" y2="142" class="a"/>
gap.cap: The floor grows and shrinks with temperature. Without the gap it buckles. Leave it at walls, cabinets, pipes, door jambs and fireplace hearths.

layout.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Plan rows so both edges are wide</text><rect x="30" y="30" width="200" height="140" class="o"/><rect x="30" y="30" width="200" height="14" class="mos"/><rect x="30" y="44" width="200" height="28" class="tl"/><rect x="30" y="72" width="200" height="28" class="tl"/><rect x="30" y="100" width="200" height="28" class="tl"/><rect x="30" y="128" width="200" height="28" class="tl"/><rect x="30" y="156" width="200" height="14" class="mos"/><line x1="90" y1="44" x2="90" y2="72" class="o"/><line x1="160" y1="44" x2="160" y2="72" class="o"/><line x1="90" y1="72" x2="90" y2="100" class="o"/><line x1="160" y1="72" x2="160" y2="100" class="o"/><line x1="90" y1="100" x2="90" y2="128" class="o"/><line x1="160" y1="100" x2="160" y2="128" class="o"/><line x1="90" y1="128" x2="90" y2="156" class="o"/><line x1="160" y1="128" x2="160" y2="156" class="o"/><text x="240" y="40">first row</text><text x="240" y="52" class="ac">{{frac(c.firstRow)}}</text><text x="240" y="150">last row</text><text x="240" y="162" class="ac">{{frac(c.lastRow)}}</text><text x="130" y="98" text-anchor="middle">full rows</text><text x="10" y="188">Ripped rows should be at least half a plank.</text>
layout.cap: If the last row comes out as a sliver, rip the first row narrower so both edges end up equal. Your numbers are on the Start tab.

click.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Angle in, then drop it flat</text><rect x="10" y="110" width="140" height="14" class="tl"/><text x="40" y="142" class="k">installed row</text><path d="M150 112 h8 v5 h-8z" class="tl"/><g><rect x="160" y="110" width="140" height="14" class="tl"/><path d="M160 115 h-10 v4 h10z" class="tl"/><animateTransform attributeName="transform" type="rotate" values="-22 160 117;-22 160 117;0 160 117;0 160 117" keyTimes="0;0.3;0.7;1" dur="3s" repeatCount="indefinite"/></g><path d="M268 52 a40 40 0 0 1 14 46" class="a" fill="none"/><polygon points="282,100 278,94 286,94" class="af"/><text x="200" y="150" class="k" text-anchor="middle">push in at 20–30°,</text><text x="200" y="162" class="k" text-anchor="middle">then lower it</text><text x="10" y="182">Tongue into groove. It clicks flat with no gap.</text>
click.title: Lock the long side
click.cap: Seat the tongue fully at an angle first, then press down. If it springs up or shows a gap, lift it and try again; never force it flat.

stagger.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Stagger end joints</text><rect x="10" y="34" width="140" height="16" class="tl"/><line x1="60" y1="34" x2="60" y2="50" class="o"/><rect x="10" y="50" width="140" height="16" class="tl"/><line x1="102" y1="50" x2="102" y2="66" class="o"/><rect x="10" y="66" width="140" height="16" class="tl"/><line x1="30" y1="66" x2="30" y2="82" class="o"/><line x1="130" y1="66" x2="130" y2="82" class="o"/><rect x="10" y="82" width="140" height="16" class="tl"/><line x1="80" y1="82" x2="80" y2="98" class="o"/><rect x="10" y="98" width="140" height="16" class="tl"/><line x1="120" y1="98" x2="120" y2="114" class="o"/><rect x="10" y="114" width="140" height="16" class="tl"/><line x1="48" y1="114" x2="48" y2="130" class="o"/><rect x="170" y="34" width="140" height="16" class="tl"/><line x1="230" y1="34" x2="230" y2="50" class="o"/><rect x="170" y="50" width="140" height="16" class="tl"/><line x1="230" y1="50" x2="230" y2="66" class="o"/><rect x="170" y="66" width="140" height="16" class="tl"/><line x1="230" y1="66" x2="230" y2="82" class="o"/><rect x="170" y="82" width="140" height="16" class="tl"/><line x1="210" y1="82" x2="210" y2="98" class="o"/><rect x="170" y="98" width="140" height="16" class="tl"/><line x1="210" y1="98" x2="210" y2="114" class="o"/><rect x="170" y="114" width="140" height="16" class="tl"/><line x1="210" y1="114" x2="210" y2="130" class="o"/><rect x="227" y="34" width="6" height="48" class="badf" fill-opacity="0.35"/><text x="10" y="148" class="gd">joints 6–8"+ apart, random</text><text x="10" y="160">no repeating pattern</text><text x="170" y="148" class="wa">H-joints / lined up</text><text x="170" y="160">weak, looks fake</text><text x="10" y="184">Use the cut-off end to start the next row.</text>
stagger.cap: Check your box for the minimum stagger; many say 6" to 8". Also avoid a stair-step pattern across rows.

tap.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Close gaps gently</text><rect x="10" y="96" width="130" height="12" class="tl"/><rect x="140" y="96" width="6" height="12" class="tl"/><path d="M146 92 h30 v20 h-30 v-6 h-4 v-8 h4z" class="w"/><rect x="184" y="90" width="40" height="8" class="bk"/><rect x="224" y="82" width="12" height="24" class="inkf"/><text x="10" y="80" class="k">tapping block</text><text x="10" y="124">on the long edge, light taps</text><line x1="10" y1="170" x2="310" y2="170" class="o"/><rect x="290" y="120" width="20" height="50" class="b"/><rect x="10" y="158" width="140" height="12" class="tl"/><rect x="152" y="158" width="132" height="12" class="tl"/><path d="M286 168 V156 H200 V138" class="o" fill="none" style="stroke-width:4"/><line x1="196" y1="134" x2="176" y2="134" class="a"/><polygon points="170,134 176,130 176,138" class="af"/><text x="208" y="150" class="k">pull bar</text><text x="30" y="142">tap this end toward the joint</text><text x="10" y="184">hook over the end by the wall, tap toward the joint</text>
tap.cap: Never hit a plank edge with a hammer: it crushes the locking edge and the joint will never close.

pipe.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Fit around a pipe</text><rect x="30" y="40" width="260" height="50" class="tl"/><line x1="30" y1="40" x2="290" y2="40" class="o"/><circle cx="160" cy="60" r="12" class="bk"/><circle cx="160" cy="60" r="7" class="inkf"/><line x1="148" y1="60" x2="148" y2="40" class="bad"/><line x1="172" y1="60" x2="172" y2="40" class="bad"/><text x="160" y="110" class="k" text-anchor="middle">hole = pipe + 1/2"</text><text x="160" y="124" text-anchor="middle">drill, then cut to the edge</text><text x="10" y="150">Fit the plank, then glue the cut-out strip</text><text x="10" y="162">back in behind the pipe. Cover with a pipe ring.</text>
pipe.cap: Measure the pipe center from the wall and from the end of the previous plank before you drill.

lastrow.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Mark the last row, plank on plank</text><rect x="10" y="28" width="300" height="18" class="b"/><text x="30" y="41">wall</text><rect x="10" y="70" width="300" height="40" class="tl"/><text x="14" y="124">last full row</text><rect x="60" y="70" width="240" height="40" class="mos"/><rect x="60" y="92" width="240" height="18" class="goodf" fill-opacity="0.35"/><rect x="60" y="52" width="240" height="40" class="tl" fill-opacity="0.75"/><rect x="60" y="52" width="240" height="40" class="o d" fill="none"/><rect x="110" y="46" width="8" height="6" class="y"/><line x1="60" y1="92" x2="300" y2="92" class="a" style="stroke-width:2"/><text x="150" y="66" class="k">B: against the spacer</text><text x="150" y="106" class="k">A: keep this strip</text><text x="10" y="146">1  Lay loose plank A exactly on the last row.</text><text x="10" y="160">2  Slide plank B over A, against the spacer.</text><text x="10" y="174">3  Draw along B onto A and cut on that line.</text><text x="10" y="188">4  The strip B did not cover is your piece.</text>
lastrow.cap: Walls are rarely straight, so mark every last-row plank this way instead of using one measurement.

trans.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Pick the right transition</text><rect x="8" y="108" width="40" height="12" class="tl"/><rect x="64" y="108" width="40" height="12" class="tl"/><line x1="8" y1="120" x2="104" y2="120" class="o"/><path d="M40 104 h32 v4 h-12 v12 h-8 v-12 h-12z" class="w"/><text x="56" y="140" class="k" text-anchor="middle">T-molding</text><text x="56" y="152" text-anchor="middle">same height</text><rect x="114" y="108" width="40" height="12" class="tl"/><rect x="170" y="116" width="40" height="4" class="tl"/><line x1="114" y1="120" x2="210" y2="120" class="o"/><path d="M146 104 h10 L184 114 v2 h-30 v4 h-8z" class="w"/><text x="162" y="140" class="k" text-anchor="middle">reducer</text><text x="162" y="152" text-anchor="middle">to lower floor</text><rect x="220" y="108" width="40" height="12" class="tl"/><rect x="276" y="104" width="40" height="16" class="tl"/><line x1="220" y1="120" x2="316" y2="120" class="o"/><path d="M252 104 h20 v4 h-12 v12 h-8z" class="w"/><text x="268" y="140" class="k" text-anchor="middle">end cap</text><text x="268" y="152" text-anchor="middle">to taller floor</text><text x="10" y="178">The molding rests on the track, never on the floor.</text>
trans.cap: The track or adhesive attaches to the subfloor only. The floating floor must slide underneath freely.

trimnail.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Nail trim to the wall, not the floor</text><rect x="246" y="20" width="40" height="150" class="b"/><rect x="10" y="150" width="300" height="20" class="w"/><rect x="10" y="138" width="232" height="12" class="tl"/><rect x="232" y="96" width="14" height="54" class="w"/><path d="M206 150 v-14 a14 14 0 0 1 14 14z" class="w"/><line x1="226" y1="112" x2="262" y2="112" class="good" style="stroke-width:2"/><circle cx="226" cy="112" r="3" class="goodf"/><line x1="204" y1="140" x2="214" y2="158" class="bad" style="stroke-width:2"/><circle cx="204" cy="140" r="3" class="badf"/><text x="16" y="60" class="gd">RIGHT: nail baseboard</text><text x="16" y="72">into the wall studs</text><text x="16" y="100" class="wa">WRONG: nail into the</text><text x="16" y="112">floor. It pins the floor.</text><text x="10" y="190">Leave a paper-thin gap under the trim.</text>
trimnail.cap: Shoe molding gets nailed into the baseboard (angled slightly up), never down into the floating floor.

saw.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Which side up? Depends on the saw</text><rect x="20" y="84" width="120" height="14" class="tl"/><rect x="20" y="96" width="120" height="3" class="af"/><text x="20" y="116" class="ac">face (down)</text><line x1="110" y1="60" x2="110" y2="124" class="o" style="stroke-width:3"/><rect x="92" y="40" width="36" height="20" class="y"/><line x1="126" y1="130" x2="126" y2="110" class="a"/><polygon points="126,108 122,114 130,114" class="af"/><text x="20" y="148" class="k">jigsaw / circular saw</text><text x="20" y="160">teeth cut upward</text><text x="20" y="172" class="wa">= cut face DOWN</text><rect x="180" y="84" width="120" height="14" class="tl"/><rect x="180" y="81" width="120" height="3" class="af"/><text x="180" y="116" class="ac">face (up)</text><circle cx="240" cy="66" r="28" class="o" fill="none"/><path d="M212 70 a28 28 0 0 0 14 22" class="a" fill="none"/><polygon points="226,95 222,89 230,89" class="af"/><text x="180" y="148" class="k">miter / table saw</text><text x="180" y="160">teeth cut downward</text><text x="180" y="172" class="gd">= cut face UP</text>
saw.cap: Teeth chip the side they exit. Put the decorative face where the teeth go in, and use a fine-tooth (60T+) or laminate blade.

layers.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">What goes under laminate</text><rect x="272" y="24" width="28" height="150" class="b"/><text x="286" y="188" text-anchor="middle">wall</text><rect x="10" y="146" width="262" height="28" class="th"/><text x="150" y="164" text-anchor="middle">concrete or plywood</text><rect x="10" y="141" width="262" height="5" class="mos"/><rect x="266" y="112" width="6" height="34" class="mos"/><rect x="10" y="137" width="110" height="4" class="mos"/><rect x="10" y="131" width="252" height="6" class="mp"/><rect x="10" y="119" width="250" height="12" class="tl"/><text x="14" y="40" class="k">laminate floats, gap at wall</text><line x1="40" y1="44" x2="40" y2="119" class="o"/><text x="80" y="60" class="k">foam underlayment (seams butted)</text><line x1="90" y1="64" x2="90" y2="131" class="o"/><text x="130" y="80" class="k">6-mil poly: on concrete</text><text x="130" y="92">(skip if built into pad)</text><line x1="180" y1="96" x2="180" y2="141" class="o"/><text x="14" y="188" class="ac">8" seam overlap, taped</text><line x1="60" y1="179" x2="60" y2="140" class="a"/><text x="262" y="106" class="ac" text-anchor="end">2" up</text>
layers.cap: Over concrete: poly first, seams overlapped 8" and taped, turned up the wall about 2". Trim it after the baseboard goes on. Over plywood, usually no poly; follow the maker.

doorbreak.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Doorways and long runs: T-molding</text><rect x="10" y="30" width="140" height="120" class="tl"/><rect x="180" y="30" width="130" height="120" class="tl"/><line x1="10" y1="30" x2="150" y2="30" class="th-l"/><line x1="180" y1="30" x2="310" y2="30" class="th-l"/><line x1="10" y1="45" x2="150" y2="45" class="th-l"/><line x1="180" y1="45" x2="310" y2="45" class="th-l"/><line x1="10" y1="60" x2="150" y2="60" class="th-l"/><line x1="180" y1="60" x2="310" y2="60" class="th-l"/><line x1="10" y1="75" x2="150" y2="75" class="th-l"/><line x1="180" y1="75" x2="310" y2="75" class="th-l"/><line x1="10" y1="90" x2="150" y2="90" class="th-l"/><line x1="180" y1="90" x2="310" y2="90" class="th-l"/><line x1="10" y1="105" x2="150" y2="105" class="th-l"/><line x1="180" y1="105" x2="310" y2="105" class="th-l"/><line x1="10" y1="120" x2="150" y2="120" class="th-l"/><line x1="180" y1="120" x2="310" y2="120" class="th-l"/><line x1="10" y1="135" x2="150" y2="135" class="th-l"/><line x1="180" y1="135" x2="310" y2="135" class="th-l"/><rect x="150" y="30" width="30" height="60" class="b"/><rect x="150" y="110" width="30" height="40" class="b"/><rect x="156" y="90" width="18" height="20" class="w"/><text x="165" y="170" class="k" text-anchor="middle">T-molding in the doorway</text><line x1="165" y1="160" x2="165" y2="112" class="a"/><text x="80" y="186" text-anchor="middle">room A</text><text x="245" y="186" text-anchor="middle">room B</text>
doorbreak.cap: Many laminate makers require a break at doorways and when a run is longer than their maximum (often 30 to 40 ft). The two floors move separately under the molding.

glossary: A floor plank with a photo layer under a hard clear wear layer, on a core of high-density wood fiber (HDF).
A floor locked to itself, not nailed or glued down, so it can move.
The thin foam or felt layer under laminate that cushions and quiets it.
A plastic sheet (6-mil poly) that stops moisture coming up from concrete.
Space left at every wall and fixed object so the floor can grow and shrink.
A T-shaped strip that covers the gap between two floors of the same height.
Abrasion class: how wear-resistant the top layer is (AC3 typical for homes).
Letting the flooring adjust to the room before installing.
Offsetting end joints from row to row.
Trimming the bottom of door casing so the floor slides under.
